Introduction

The Cox Proportional Hazards model is a regression method used to analyze the relationships between variables and the time until a specific event occurs. Survival analysis accounts for both the occurrence of an event and the length of time before the event, while accounting for censored observations. The Cox model expresses an individual’s hazard at time (t) as
λ(t׀X) = λ0(t)exp (β’ • X), where λ0 is the baseline hazard, β’ is a vector of regression coefficients, and X is a vector of time-fixed covariates (Bellera et al. 2010). Exponentiating a coefficient produces a hazard ratio, which describes the relative risk of experiencing the event while holding other variables constant. A hazard ratio greater than one indicates an increased risk. For example, Cox models have been used to study the duration of the birth process (Wuryandari et al. 2018), the time until farmers are willing to pay agricultural insurance premiums (Hidayat et al. 2022), website drop-offs (Soobramoney et al. 2023), credit default (Dirick et al. 2017), and survival following cancer treatments (Abadi et al. 2014). These applications demonstrate how the model can be used when the outcome of interest involves the time until a specified event. The general process for conducting a Cox proportional hazards analysis is 1. Define the event of interest, survival time, and censoring indicator, 2. Select the explanatory variables that may affect the event hazard, 3. Fit the Cox proportional hazards model and estimate its coefficients, 4. Convert the coefficients into hazard ratios and calculate their confidence intervals, 5. Test whether the proportional hazards assumption is satisfied, 6. Evaluate model fit and interpret the estimated effects within the context of the research question (Lee 2023).

The central assumption of the Cox model is that the hazard ratio associated with a predictor remains constant throughout the observation period. In other words, the model assumes that the hazards for two individuals or groups are proportional over time. The assumption can be evaluated using Kaplan-Meier curves, log-minus-log plots, Schoenfeld residuals, or interactions between predictors and time. However, reviews of pediatric leukemia and total joint arthroplasty research found that the proportional hazards assumption was frequently unreported or poorly evaluated (Ilari Kuitunen 2021); (Ilari Kuitunen 2023). Time-varying effects should be investigated as a regular part of Cox regression analysis rather than assuming that proportionality automatically holds (Bellera et al. 2010).

One limitation of the Cox proportional hazards model is its assumption that the hazard ratio for each predictor remains constant throughout the study period. If a predictor has a stronger effect at one point in time than another, this assumption is violated. The model may then produce a single hazard ratio that does not accurately represent the changing relationship. Researchers should therefore test the proportional hazards assumption before interpreting the model’s results. When the assumption is violated, modifications such as stratifying the model or including time-dependent effects may be necessary. The performance of these approaches can vary according to the sample size, censoring rate, and distribution of survival times (Iketle et al. 2024). Although the Cox proportional hazards model is flexible, reliable results depend on properly accounting for censored observations and verifying that the proportional hazards assumption is appropriate.

Literature Review

Cox PH model across domains

Empirical studies have shown that the Cox PH model can be used well beyond its origin in clinical survival analysis. The studies reviewed for this project applied the model to academic performance, childbirth, agricultural economics, website use, and credit risk. Thus, the model could be used in any setting that has time-to-event data with censoring. In a study on medical student attrition, a stepwise Cox model was used to examine which academic and demographic factors predicted when a student would experience academic difficulty. Researchers found that curriculum track, MCAT verbal reasoning scores, and early course failures were the strongest predictors, and that the risk peaked at a specific point in the training timeline (Chau-Kuang 2010). In a study on the duration of childbirth, Cox PH was used to examine whether a specific birth-preparation method changed the time it took to deliver. The study found that this method significantly shortened the time to delivery compared to standard practice (Wuryandari et al. 2018). (Hidayat et al. 2022) applied Cox PH to model economic behavior, using the Efron partial-likelihood method and stepwise variable selection to examine how long it took rice farmers to pay an agricultural insurance premium. They found that education level, off-farm employment, and production costs affected how quickly farmers acted.(Soobramoney et al. 2023) treated website user drop-off as a survival problem, in which “survival” meant viewing at least three pages. Both Cox PH and a survival random forest model were used, and browser type, landing page, and search-referral status were found to be key hazards. This shows that the framework is not limited to health and social science, and it can be applied to behavioral and business data as well. Together, these studies show that all the model needs is a duration variable and a binary event or censoring indicator. Also, the Cox model can flexiby handle multiple covariates. Therefore, it is a tool that could be useful wherever the timing of an outcome is of interest. For these reasons, Cox PH was chosen for the recidivism data in this study, which has this same time-to-event structure.

Proportional hazards assumption

Another theme in the literature is that researchers should test that a covariate’s effect on hazard stays constant over time. (Bellera et al. 2010) warned that predictors can look strong early in follow-up and then weaken considerably over time. Using Schoenfeld residuals, they showed that hormone receptor status in breast cancer patients had this kind of time-varying effect. A standard Cox model would have hidden this finding. (Abadi et al. 2014) reached a similar conclusion in a separate and larger breast cancer survival study. They found that the proportional hazards assumption held differently across age and cancer-stage subgroups and fitting stratified Cox models to account for this difference between the groups. Also, (Lee 2023) made the same point in a more general methodological review. This review noted that hazard or survival curves that overlap on a graph are a practical sign that the PH assumption has been violated. Failing to detect a violation could lead to misleading conclusions about the true relationship between a covariate and the outcome. For recidivism data, a covariate’s effect on the hazard of reincarceration could be concentrated in the early months, therefore the proportional hazards assumption will be tested.

Handling non-proportional hazards

Several reviewed studies compared modified Cox specifications designed to address PH violations. (Iketle et al. 2024) compared the stratified Cox model, which allows a different baseline hazard for each level of a violating covariate, against the extended Cox model, which puts time-varying covariates directly into the hazard function. This was done using Monte Carlo simulations across different censoring rates, sample sizes, and survival distributions. They found that the extended model performed better than the stratified model when a true time-varying effect was present. However, they noted that there were practical limitations in specifying the correct functional form for that time dependence. (M. S. K and Murugan 2024) emphasized that the Cox model’s main value was that it could isolate each covariate’s independent contribution to hazard while controlling for the others. However, they cautioned that the PH assumption itself, along with the interpretation of complex covariate interactions, remained a limitations of this approach. (Dirick et al. 2017) took this comparative approach even further in a credit-risk context. They benchmarked Cox PH against accelerated failure time models, spline-based Cox extensions, and mixture cure models (designed to account for a subpopulation that will never experience the event at all) across ten datasets. This study found that Cox PH with penalized splines consistently outperformed fully parametric alternatives, reinforcing the model’s flexibility even when covariate-hazard relationships are nonlinear.

Overall, the Cox PH is well suited to the structure of the Iowa data. This study will begin with a standard Cox PH model, tests the proportional hazards assumption formally using Schoenfeld residuals, and addresses any violations dectected through stratification or time-varying covariate specifications.

Methods

  • Detail the models or algorithms used.

  • Justify your choices based on the problem and data.

The common non-parametric regression model is \(Y_i = m(X_i) + \varepsilon_i\), where \(Y_i\) can be defined as the sum of the regression function value \(m(x)\) for \(X_i\). Here \(m(x)\) is unknown and \(\varepsilon_i\) some errors. With the help of this definition, we can create the estimation for local averaging i.e. \(m(x)\) can be estimated with the product of \(Y_i\) average and \(X_i\) is near to \(x\). In other words, this means that we are discovering the line through the data points with the help of surrounding data points. The estimation formula is printed below (R Core Team 2019):

\[ M_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} W_n (X_i) Y_i \tag{1} \]\(W_n(x)\) is the sum of weights that belongs to all real numbers. Weights are positive numbers and small if \(X_i\) is far from \(x\).

Another equation:

\[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 +\varepsilon_i \]

Code 
# loading packages 
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(ggthemes)
library(ggrepel)
library(dslabs)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(skimr)
Code 
# Load Data
data_raw <- read_csv("ipr_dataset.csv", na = c("", "NA"))

# Data Cleaning
empty_cols <- names(data_raw)[colSums(is.na(data_raw)) == nrow(data_raw)]
data_raw <- data_raw %>% select(-all_of(empty_cols))

df <- data_raw %>%
  mutate(
    event = if_else(!is.na(days_to_recid), 1, 0),
    release_date = as.Date(exit_sup_end_date),
    time_days = if_else(event == 1, days_to_recid, 1095)
  )

df <- df %>% mutate(time_days = if_else(time_days == 0, 0.5, time_days))

df <- df %>%
  unite("exit_combined", exit_type, exit_subtype, sep = " - ", remove = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(
    sex           = factor(sex),
    Race          = factor(Race),
    exit_type     = factor(exit_type),
    exit_sup      = factor(exit_sup),
    risk_ranking  = factor(
      if_else(is.na(risk_ranking), "Not assessed", risk_ranking),
      levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High", "Not assessed")
    ),
    age_c         = age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(sex))
Code 
df %>%
  filter(event == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = survival_time_months)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#d1495b", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "When Does Reincarceration Occur?",
       x = "Months to reincarceration", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
Code 
set.seed(20)  

pt <- df %>%
  slice_sample(n = 20) %>%
  arrange(time_days) %>%
  mutate(id = row_number())

plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1200), ylim = c(0.5, 20.5),
     xlab = "Days since release", ylab = "Individual", yaxt = "n",
     main = "Time to Reincarceration: Events vs. Censoring")
axis(2, at = 1:20, labels = paste0("P", 1:20), cex.axis = 0.7)
abline(v = 1095, lty = 2, col = "grey60")            
text(1095, 20.4, "3-yr cutoff", pos = 2, col = "grey40", cex = 0.8)

for (i in 1:20) {
  segments(0, pt$id[i], pt$time_days[i], pt$id[i], col = "#3a86d4", lwd = 3)
  if (pt$event[i] == 1) {
    points(pt$time_days[i], pt$id[i], pch = 19, col = "#d1495b", cex = 1.4)   
  } else {
    points(pt$time_days[i], pt$id[i], pch = ">", col = "#3a86d4", cex = 1.4) 
  }
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("recidivated (event)", "censored (no return by cutoff)"),
       pch = c(19, 62), col = c("#d1495b", "#3a86d4"))
Code 
km_risk <- survfit(Surv(time_days, event) ~ risk_ranking, data = df)

plot(km_risk, col = c("#2a9d8f", "#e9c46a", "#d1495b", "grey60"), lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Days since release", ylab = "Probability of remaining in community",
     main = "Time to Reincarceration by Risk Classification")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2,
       legend = levels(df$risk_ranking),
       col = c("#2a9d8f", "#e9c46a", "#d1495b", "grey60"))
